t: Nobody invented this. Bacteria have been using it against viruses for billions of years.
CRISPR was not designed. It was found — an immune system bacteria have been running against viruses for a very long time, noticed by people studying something else entirely.
sub: It was discovered by people studying salt-tolerant microbes and yoghurt cultures.
Nobody involved was looking for a gene-editing tool, and that is worth sitting with.

question: Bacteria get infected by viruses too. What would a defence need to do?
What would a bacterial adaptive immune system require?
options: Keep a record of past attackers and recognise them again
stages.outcome: Keep a record of past attackers and recognise them again
note: Commit. You have met recognise-remember-respond before, in an animal. This is the same problem for something with no cells to spare.

t: Put the steps of a bacterium's memory in order.
The CRISPR system in its native role. Match each step.

parts.label: Keep a piece of the virus

label: Survive an attack and keep evidence
Acquisition: a fragment of the invader is retained
Add it to the list of known enemies
The spacer is inserted into the CRISPR array
Turn the list into search terms
Array is transcribed and processed into guide RNAs
Destroy anything on the list
Interference: matching invader DNA is cleaved

t: The library of past attackers is called a CRISPR array, and it is a bacterium's memory.
The CRISPR array is a genuine adaptive immune system: acquired, specific, heritable, and stored as sequence.
Acquisition, expression and interference — the same three phases as vertebrate adaptive immunity, implemented in DNA rather than in cell populations.

It differs from your immune system in one striking way: the memory is written into the genome and inherited by every descendant. A bacterium that survives an infection passes the immunity on, which is Lamarckian in form — acquired characteristics genuinely being inherited — and one of very few real instances.
sub: The spacers are a record of what that bacterium's ancestors survived.
Reading the array tells you which viruses that lineage has met, in order, like tree rings.
Which is what made it recognisable: the sequences between the repeats matched known viruses, and that was the clue that solved it.

The array had been described in 1987 and sat unexplained for eighteen years. The insight in 2005 was that the spacers matched phage sequences — and the function fell out immediately. The data had been public the whole time; what was missing was the comparison.

q: What is CRISPR actually for, in a bacterium?
What is the native function of the CRISPR system?
In what sense is it an adaptive immune system?
options: Recognising and destroying viruses it has met before
why: It is a defence. The bacterium keeps a piece of every virus that attacked it, and uses those pieces to recognise and cut up the same virus next time.

Antiviral defence. Fragments of past invaders are stored as spacers and used to generate guides that destroy matching sequences on re-infection — acquisition, memory and specific response, which is what adaptive means.

It satisfies every criterion: the response is specific to a particular invader, it is acquired from experience rather than pre-existing, and it persists as memory. It is also heritable, which vertebrate adaptive immunity is not — the memory is in the genome rather than in a cell population.

t: The most powerful tool in biology came from people studying yoghurt.

The system was worked out substantially by researchers at a food company trying to stop viruses ruining yoghurt cultures. Nobody in that work was pursuing gene editing, and nobody could have proposed it as a goal. It is one of the better arguments for funding people to follow odd questions, and it is a more honest version of that argument than most, because the useful application was genuinely unforeseeable rather than merely unfashionable.
